drills.q: What does the log scaling in TF-IDF's term-frequency component prevent?
drills.a: It prevents raw repetition count from linearly inflating a document's score -- a document saying a word 40 times isn't 40x more relevant than one saying it once; log-scaling captures diminishing returns.

drills.q: Why can lemmatization not run correctly without a POS tagger upstream?
drills.a: The correct lemma depends on part of speech -- 'meeting' lemmatizes to 'meet' as a verb but stays 'meeting' as a noun. Without POS context the lemmatizer guesses and gets ambiguous words wrong.

drills.q: Derive why BM25's k1 parameter produces term-frequency saturation while raw log-scaled TF-IDF does not.
drills.a: BM25's tf component is tf*(k1+1)/(tf+k1*(1-b+b*|d|/avgdl)), which approaches a hard ceiling of k1+1 as tf->infinity. Log-scaled TF (1+log(count)) keeps growing without bound, just more slowly -- it's a softer, unbounded version of saturation.

drills.q: A production TF-IDF classifier's accuracy drops sharply after a new content batch ships. Walk through the diagnosis.
drills.a: Suspect vocabulary drift first: the fitted vocabulary from training doesn't cover new terms (new brand names, slang), so those tokens are silently dropped at transform time. Check the out-of-vocabulary rate on incoming documents as a leading indicator, then refit on a rolling recent window and retrain together as one versioned unit.

drills.q: Explain UAS vs LAS and why a rule-based extraction pipeline should care about LAS specifically.
drills.a: UAS is percent correct head attachment; LAS additionally requires the correct relation label. Extraction rules key off specific relation labels (dobj, nsubj, amod) -- a parser with high UAS but weak LAS attaches the right words together but mislabels the relationship the rule is matching on, silently breaking extraction even though structure looks right.

drills.q: Why did BPE tokenization replace whitespace tokenization inside neural models specifically, not just as a preference?
drills.a: Whitespace tokenization with a fixed vocabulary maps any unseen word to a generic <UNK> token, losing information. BPE decomposes any string into known subword or byte-level pieces greedily merged by frequency, so there is no true out-of-vocabulary case -- essential for open-vocabulary generation and multilingual/morphologically rich text.

drills.q: Your TF-IDF+linear classifier and a fine-tuned transformer are within 1.5 F1 points on a content-tagging task at high volume. Which do you ship, and what would change your mind?
drills.a: Ship the linear model by default -- at production volume the latency/infra cost gap (single-digit ms CPU vs tens of ms GPU) usually dwarfs a 1.5-point F1 gain, and feature weights are directly inspectable. Change the answer if the gap sits on a business-critical boundary (compliance-relevant moderation) or the task needs context bag-of-words can't represent (negation, long-range dependency).

drills.q: Design the preprocessing pipeline for a multilingual content corpus spanning English, Spanish, German, and Japanese.
drills.a: Tokenization can't be one regex: Japanese needs a dedicated segmenter (no whitespace boundaries), German compounds need subword tokenization or a compound-splitter to avoid vocabulary explosion, Spanish needs its own stemmer/accent normalization. At scale, a jointly-trained multilingual subword tokenizer (SentencePiece) feeding a multilingual model beats maintaining four separate classical pipelines -- but classical stemming/lemmatization resource maturity is genuinely uneven across languages and that's a real constraint to name.

drills.q: A dependency-parse-based extraction rule that worked for a year starts failing on 15% of documents overnight. Diagnose it.
drills.a: First check whether the parser model/library was upgraded -- dependency label sets and attachment conventions can shift subtly between versions, silently breaking rules keyed to specific relation labels. Second check for input distribution shift (new content source, different sentence structure). Prevent recurrence by pinning the parser model version and running a regression suite of known sentence-to-extraction pairs on every upgrade.

drills.q: Why is stemming acceptable for an internal search index but risky for a customer-facing field, using a concrete failure example?
drills.a: Stemming can produce non-words (running->runn under aggressive rules) and over-stem, merging distinct words to the same stem (organic and organization colliding), which is invisible in an internal match-only index but shows up as garbled text or irrelevant results the moment it's displayed or matched against a controlled vocabulary the user sees.
